claim: An owner who believes property is valued too high or improperly valued/listed may file a petition with the county assessor on the department-prescribed form.
The petition to the assessor must be filed within 60 days after the assessor mailed the notice of valuation (or amended notice); USPS postmark is evidence of filing date.
The petition must state the owner's opinion of full cash value and substantial information (income, market or cost approach).

If the assessor denies relief in whole or part, the petitioner has 25 days after the decision is mailed to appeal to the county board of equalization (or state board if no county board) or to superior court.
An owner may not appear before the county or state board of equalization without first filing the assessor petition, and may not raise issues not included in it.
Class three (owner-occupied residential) property is assessed at ten percent of full cash value or limited valuation.

Arizona's homestead exemption protects up to $400,000 of equity in a primary residence from attachment, execution and forced sale (adjusted annually for CPI beginning January 1, 2024).
Only one homestead exemption may be held by a married couple or a single person; claimant must be 18 or older and reside in Arizona.
The homestead exemption automatically attaches to identifiable cash sale proceeds for 18 months after sale or until a new homestead is established, whichever is shorter.

Property tax exemption exists for widows/widowers, persons with total and permanent disability and veterans with disabilities, with income and assessment limits; claimed by affidavit with the county assessor.

The primary residence of a veteran with a 100 percent service-connected disability rating is fully exempt from property tax; conveying title to another owner is a disqualifying event for these exemptions.

Arizona statute exempts a list of instruments and transfers from the affidavit (of property value) and fee requirement, including deeds of gift, court-ordered conveyances, and quitclaim deeds for no monetary consideration.

Exempt transfers include trustee's deeds under power of sale, sales for delinquent taxes, transfers between spouses/parent-child/grandparent-grandchild/siblings with nominal consideration, and beneficiary deeds with nominal consideration.
An instrument describing an exempt transaction must note the specific exemption claimed on its face at recording.
The Arizona Department of Revenue's Summary of Arizona Taxes lists personal income, transaction privilege, use, property, and vehicle license taxes and does not list a real estate transfer tax.

A trustee holding a deed of trust has a power of sale (non-judicial foreclosure); at the beneficiary's option a trust deed may instead be foreclosed judicially like a mortgage.
A trustee's sale may not occur before the 91st day after the notice of sale is recorded, and not on a Saturday or legal holiday.

Notice of trustee's sale must be recorded, mailed per 33-809, posted on the property at least 20 days before sale, and published once a week for four consecutive weeks with the last publication at least 10 days before sale.
Trustor defenses are waived unless a Rule 65 court order stopping the sale is obtained before 5:00 p.m. MST on the last business day before the sale.
The trustee's deed conveys title absolutely without right of redemption after a trustee's sale; high bidder must pay by 5:00 p.m. the next business day.

No deficiency action may be maintained after a trustee's sale of 2.5 acres or less limited to a single one- or two-family dwelling (for loans originated after 12/31/2014 exceptions apply for builder/never-completed/never-occupied dwellings).
Deficiency actions where allowed must be brought within 90 days after the trustee's sale.

A judgment creditor may have a writ of execution issued within ten years after entry of judgment (or renewal).
A judgment debtor or successor may redeem property sold on execution within six months after the sale date (30 days if the court found the property abandoned and not agricultural/grazing).
Lienholders subsequent to the judgment may redeem within five days after the debtor's period ends, in order of priority, paying the sale price plus 8 percent additions per 12-1285.
Persons entitled to redeem are the judgment debtor or successor in interest and creditors with a junior judgment or mortgage lien.
A purchase-money mortgage foreclosure judgment on a one- or two-family dwelling of 2.5 acres or less cannot be satisfied from other property of the debtor.

Successors may collect personal property by affidavit 30 days after death if no personal representative is pending and personal property (less liens) does not exceed $200,000.

Affidavit of succession to real property may be filed not sooner than six months after death if no PR is pending/appointed and real property in Arizona (less liens) does not exceed $300,000 by full cash value at death.

The real-property affidavit requires funeral/last-illness expenses and unsecured debts paid, successor entitled by intestacy/will/allowance, no other claimant, and no federal estate tax due; a certified death certificate is attached.
The affidavit is filed in the superior court of the county of domicile with the normal filing fee (waivable), and the registrar's certified copy is recorded with the county recorder.
A purchaser from or lender to the successor named in a recorded certified affidavit receives the same protection as one dealing with a distributee under a PR deed of distribution.

Recording fee for government-party instruments recorded at government request is $15 per instrument.
Certified copies cost $1 per page plus $3 for the certificate and seal.
A recorder may accept digitized images of recordable instruments from title insurers/agents, banks, active State Bar members, federal agencies, trusted submitters or governmental entities.
Instruments are recorded consecutively by time received, and recording is done at the county recorder of the county where the property sits.
Maricopa County Recorder charges no additional fee for electronic recording beyond standard recording fees.

Deeds that confirm or correct a previously recorded deed, and name-change deeds, are exempt from the affidavit and fee.

A deed where the grantor holds title as trustee must disclose the names and addresses of the trust beneficiaries; failure makes the conveyance voidable by the other party within two years of recording.

Property tax on real property is a lien on the assessed property that attaches January 1 of the tax year.
The tax lien is prior and superior to all other liens except state liens and liens for taxes of other years.
The lien is removed only when taxes, penalties and interest are paid, title vests in a tax-sale purchaser, or a certificate of removal and abatement issues.
Property taxes are due in two halves, October 1 and March 1; the first half is delinquent after November 1 at 5:00 p.m. and the second after May 1 at 5:00 p.m.
The county treasurer secures delinquent taxes by selling the tax liens and foreclosing the right to redeem.

Arizona sells tax liens (certificates of purchase) rather than deeds at the first stage; the treasurer later forecloses the right to redeem.
A real property tax lien may be fully redeemed within three years after the tax lien sale, and after three years until a treasurer's deed is delivered.
The county treasurer must mail notice of proposed sale to the owner of each parcel on the delinquent tax list at the last known address.

In a foreclosure of the right to redeem, a court may order an excess proceeds sale if the property would likely sell for more than $2,500 above the lien-holder's amounts; the lien holder's amounts accrue interest at 16 percent per annum.
After judgment foreclosing the right to redeem, the owner has no further right, title or interest, subject to appeal; easements and certain assessment liens survive.

For nonpayment, landlord gives written notice and tenant has five days to pay before the landlord may file a special detainer action.
For material noncompliance, landlord gives written notice terminating the lease not less than ten days after receipt if not remedied in ten days (five days for health and safety breaches).
Special detainer summons issues the day the complaint is filed with a hearing not more than six nor less than three days from the summons date.
Before filing, a lease is reinstated if the tenant pays all past due rent and a reasonable late fee; after filing, tenant must also pay attorney fees and court costs.

A forcible detainer exists when a tenant retains possession after tenancy ends or after written demand; certain unauthorized occupants may be removed after a reasonable request to leave, with writ of restitution issued immediately after judgment.
A justice court eviction action may claim up to $10,000, excluding interest, costs and attorneys' fees.

Arizona allows a beneficiary deed that expressly states it is effective on the owner's death and transfers the interest to the designated grantee beneficiary.
A beneficiary deed is valid only if executed and recorded with the county recorder before the owner's death.
The owner may revoke at any time by a recorded revocation; signature or consent of the grantee beneficiary is not required during the owner's life.
The transfer is subject to all conveyances, mortgages, liens and encumbrances made by the owner during life; the last recorded beneficiary deed controls.
A beneficiary deed is not revoked by a later will, and may name multiple grantees or a successor grantee beneficiary.
A beneficiary deed with only nominal consideration is exempt from the affidavit of property value and fee.
